title: 45-Day Identification Strategy
name: 45-Day Identification Strategy
metaTitle: 45-Day Identification Strategy in San Diego, CA
metaDescription: 45-day identification strategy for San Diego 1031 exchanges, grounded in real screening work rather than a letter filed on time to check a box.

sections.html: Forty-five calendar days sounds like enough time until you are trying to screen replacement candidates in a San Diego market where a defense-adjacent industrial building or a Kearny Mesa flex unit can go under contract before you have finished reviewing the rent roll. The clock starts the day the relinquished property closes and does not pause for a slow lender, a holiday week, or a seller who takes three days to respond to an offer.

sections.heading: What a 45-Day Package Usually Skips
sections.html: A lot of "45-day identification" quotes in this market cover one task: making sure the letter itself is filled out correctly and delivered to the qualified intermediary on time. That is the easy part. The hard part, actually screening candidates for financing, title, and seller motivation inside a five-week window, is often left to the investor to figure out alone, which is how people end up naming a property on day 44 that they have not actually vetted.

sections.heading: Why the Clock Is Tighter in a Supply-Constrained Market
sections.html: San Diego's employment base around the Navy, defense contractors, and biotech tenants near Torrey Pines and UTC keeps demand steady for the same handful of industrial and office-lab buildings that come up for sale. A property that looks available on day one can be in escrow with another buyer by day ten. Waiting until week five to start seriously screening candidates means competing for whatever is left, not what was actually the best fit.

sections.heading: The Screening Sequence That Fits Inside 45 Days
sections.html:
We run candidates through the same sequence every time, front-loaded into the first two weeks so there is room left to react if a top choice falls through. That sequence covers:

  • Preliminary title pull on every serious candidate
  • Lender feasibility check against your exchange basis and timeline
  • Seller motivation and closing-timeline confirmation
  • Rent roll or lease abstract review for income property
  • Fair market value check against the 200% ceiling if more than three names are involved

sections.heading: Naming a Backup Without Wasting the List
sections.html: Every serious San Diego identification letter needs at least one real backup, not a filler name added to look thorough. The three-property and 200% rules both allow room for a second candidate, and a genuinely vetted backup is what keeps a fallen-through deal from turning into a failed exchange. Confirm the specific rule you are using and its limits with your qualified intermediary before finalizing the letter.

sections.heading: What a Bargain 45-Day Package Actually Buys You
sections.html:
A low-cost identification package typically covers the letter itself, correctly formatted and delivered to the deadline. It does not typically cover a lender feasibility check, a title pull, or a call to confirm a seller's actual willingness to close on the exchange timeline. Those omissions are easy to miss when comparing quotes side by side, because a bare letter and a fully screened letter look identical on the invoice line.

The difference shows up later, usually in week five, when a name on the letter turns out to be a property that was never actually financeable or available. At that point there is no time left to add a properly screened replacement, which is the exact scenario the identification rules are supposed to protect against.

A useful test before you commit to a package is asking exactly which of the screening steps, title, lender feasibility, seller confirmation, are included at the quoted price, and which would be billed separately if a candidate needed deeper review. A provider who cannot answer specifically is telling you something about how much screening actually happens before a name reaches your letter.

The same question applies to timing. Ask when screening actually starts relative to the relinquished-property closing, since a provider who waits until the letter is due to begin real diligence is running the same five-week gauntlet the investor would be running alone, just with an extra fee attached.

The providers worth working with in this market front-load the calendar deliberately, treating the first two weeks as the working window and the last two as a buffer for negotiation and confirmation, rather than the reverse.

That front-loaded pace is what actually gives an investor room to walk away from a candidate that fails screening and still have time to bring a real replacement forward before day 45.

faqs.q: When does the 45-day clock actually start?
faqs.a: The day the relinquished property closes, in calendar days, and it runs whether or not you have started looking at replacement candidates yet.

faqs.q: Is filing the identification letter on time enough to protect the exchange?
faqs.a: No. The letter has to name real property under one of the identification rules, and if none of the identified properties are financeable or available, filing on time does not save the exchange.

faqs.q: Why does San Diego's market make the 45 days feel shorter than in other cities?
faqs.a: Steady demand from defense, Navy, and biotech-adjacent tenants means the buildings that fit an exchange budget move fast. Waiting until late in the window to screen candidates usually means picking from what is left over.

faqs.q: Can I change my identified properties after the letter is filed?
faqs.a: You can amend or revoke an identification any time before the 45th day ends, but not after. After that date the list is locked for that exchange.

faqs.q: How many properties should actually be on the letter?
faqs.a: Enough to cover a real fallback if your top choice falls through, without padding the list with names you have not screened. Three well-vetted candidates usually beat eight unvetted ones.
